title: Growing sweet cicely
subtitle: A tall, anise-scented perennial with edible leaves, seeds, and roots.
excerpt: Sweet cicely is a large perennial herb with fern-like leaves and a sweet anise flavour. It is one of the first plants to appear in spring and is useful as a sugar substitute in cooking. It grows well in shade and tolerates dry soils once established.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). Sweetening properties from food history sources including Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861). UK hardiness and growing conditions widely documented.

glossaryTerms.definition: A period of cold and moisture that breaks dormancy in certain seeds. Seeds of sweet cicely, hawthorn, and many other plants will not germinate without it. In practice: sow fresh seed in autumn outside or refrigerate seed in damp compost for six to eight weeks before spring sowing.

content.text: Sweet cicely is one of the most shade-tolerant perennial vegetables available in the UK. The feathery leaves emerge in February, weeks before most garden plants. They taste of anise and are mildly sweet. Use them in fruit salads, rhubarb dishes, and herb teas.

to germinate. The most reliable method is to sow fresh seed outside in autumn and leave the pots outside over winter. Germination happens in spring. Bought dried seed often fails; fresh seed from a known plant is much more reliable.

Sweet cicely thrives in partial to full shade and in any reasonably fertile soil. It grows well under trees and in north-facing borders. It reaches 1 to 1.5 m in full growth and dies back completely in winter. Hardy to H7 and fully frost-tolerant.

Harvest young leaves from March onwards. The green, unripe seeds in May and June are crunchy and strongly anise-flavoured. The ripe seeds in July are hard and less useful for eating but dry well and keep their flavour. The roots are also edible, cooked as a root vegetable, but harvesting roots kills the plant.
Cut the flower stems before they set seed if you want to prevent the plant spreading. Sweet cicely self-seeds readily in moist, shady conditions and can become weedy in a small garden.

attrs.title: Sweet cicely with rhubarb
attrs.body: Add two or three sweet cicely leaves to a pot of rhubarb as it cooks. The natural sweetness in the leaves reduces the amount of sugar needed in the recipe. This is not a dramatic effect but is enough to cut the usual sugar quantity by about a third without any change in flavour.
